subject: Back Pay
title: PERC BP-2015-010 Final Order (Back Pay)

STATE OF FLORIDA
PUBLIC EMPLOYEES RELATIONS COMMISSION
LAWRENCE YOUNG,
Employee, Case No. BP- 2015 -010
(Relates to CS- 2015 -029)
v.
FINAL ORDER
DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTIONS,
: Order Number: 15CS -156
Date Issued: October 19, 2015
Agency.
Michael Braverman, Fort Lauderdale, attorney representing employee.
Sena M. Bailes, Tallahassee, attorney representing agency.
On June 30, 2015, the Public Employees Relations Commission (Commission)
issued an order vacating Lawrence Young's dismissal by the Department of Corrections
(Agency). The Agency was directed to reinstate Young and to provide him with back
pay and benefits, less any compensation and earnings which he would not have
received had his employment with the Agency not been interrupted. On the same date,
this back pay case was established. On July 15, a hearing officer was appointed to
determine the amount of back pay and an evidentiary hearing was scheduled.
On September 1, a telephone hearing was conducted between Tallahassee and
West Palm Beach. On September 16, the hearing officer issued his recommended
order concluding that Young had mitigated his job loss under the requirements outlined
in Vickery v. Department of Corrections, 30 FCSR 79 (2015), during the back pay
period. He further concluded that Young is entitled to gross back pay of $12,709.28,

BP-2015-010
(Relates to CS-2015-029)
minus taxes and other lawful deductions, plus $1,299.88 for health insurance costs.
Neither party filed exceptions to the hearing officer's recommended order or a transcript
of the back pay hearing.
We accept the hearing officer's findings of fact. Furthermore, we agree with the
hearing officer's analysis of the dispositive legal issues, his conclusions of law, and his
recommendations. Therefore, the hearing officer's recommended order is incorporated
herein. § 120.57(1)(1), Fla. Stat. (2015).
Based on the foregoing, the Agency is directed to pay Young back pay in the
amount of $12,709.28, minus appropriate deductions, plus $1,299.88 for health
insurance costs, plus interest at the lawful rate until paid. Accordingly, this back pay
case is closed.
This order and the Commission's June 30, 2015, Order Vacating Agency Action
may be appealed to the appropriate district court of appeal. A notice of appeal must be
received by the Commission and the district court of appeal within thirty days from the
date of this order. Except in cases of indigency, the court will require a filing fee and
the Commission will require payment for preparing the record on appeal. Further
explanation of the right to appeal is provided in Sections 120.68 and 447.504, Florida
Statutes (2015), and the Florida Rules of Appellate Procedure.

PUBLIC EMPLOYEES RELATIONS COMMISSION
LAWRENCE YOUNG,
Employee, Case No. BP- 2015 -010
(Relates to CS- 2015 -029)
v.
HEARING OFFICER'S
DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTIONS, RECOMMENDED ORDER
:
Agency.
Michael Braverman, Fort Lauderdale, attorney representing employee.
Sena M. Bailes, Tallahassee, attorney representing agency.
MORTON, Hearing Officer.
On June 30, 2015, the Commission issued an order directing the Department of
Corrections (Agency) to reinstate Lawrence Young and provide him with back pay and
benefits, less any compensation and earnings he would not have received had his
employment with the Agency not been interrupted. See Young v. Department of
Corrections, Order No. 15CS -106 (PERC 2015). The Commission's Clerk opened a back
pay case based on the Commission's order. On July 8, Young filed his computation of
back pay on PERC Form 18.
On September 1, after due notice and without objection, a telephone hearing was
conducted between Tallahassee and West Palm Beach. All parties were afforded the
opportunity to call witnesses, cross -examine witnesses, and fully participate.' Young
entered three exhibits into evidence and he testified on his own behalf. The Agency did
'This case was consolidated for hearing with Alston v. Department of Corrections,
Case No. BP- 2015 -011. While the underlying disciplinary cases were based on the same
occurrences, for purposes of clarity, I am issuing separate back pay recommended
orders.

BP-2015-010
(Relates to CS-2015-029)
not offer any exhibits or witness testimony. The parties filed written post -hearing
arguments, which I have carefully considered in preparing this recommended order. A
transcript of the hearing was not filed.
During the hearing, the parties arrived at a number of stipulated facts, which I have
included in my findings of fact below. The material dispute of fact necessitating the
hearing revolved around how much back pay Young was entitled to receive and whether
he should be reimbursed for the out of pocket costs he paid to obtain health insurance.
FINDINGS OF FACT
Based on the record as a whole, I make the following findings:
1. Young was terminated effective February 17, 2015. The Commission
issued its Order Vacating Agency Action on June 30. Young returned to duty with the
Agency on July 17. The total back pay exposure period is February 17, 2015, through
and including July 16, 2015. (Stipulation)
2. Prior to his dismissal, Young was employed as a Correctional Probation
Officer in the West Palm Beach Circuit Office.
3. Young worked an eight hour workday /forty hour workweek schedule. His
gross wages were $18.99 hourly or $1,518.71 bi- weekly. (Stipulation)2
2There is a slight discrepancy between the bi- weekly amount calculated from the
hourly amount and the stipulated bi- weekly amount. ($18.99 per hour x 40 hours a week
x 2 weeks = $1.519.20 verses stipulated bi- weekly amount of $1,518.71). Because the
calculations include partial weeks and the need to consider daily amounts, I have used
2

BP-2015-010
(Relates to CS-2015-029)
4. The initial grace period lasted from February 17, through and including
March 18. (Stipulation)3
5. Young did not take a disbursement from the Florida Retirement System and
he is eligible for reinstatement in the Florida Retirement System. (Stipulation)
6. There were twenty -two work days during the initial grace period. Young is
entitled to $3,342.24 in gross back pay, less taxes and any other lawful deductions, for
the initial grace period.
7. Young is also entitled to back pay for the second grace period, which
started on June 30, when the Commission entered its Order Vacating Agency Action and
July 17, when he returned to work. June 30 was a Tuesday, so Young is also entitled to
receive back pay for Monday, June 29, pursuant to recent changes in Commission case
law.4
8. There were fourteen work days during the second grace period. Young is
entitled to $2,126.88 in gross back pay, less taxes and any other lawful deductions, for
the second grace period.
the stipulated hourly amount in making my calculations. Any difference between the two
is negligible.
Pursuant to well -established case law, an employee is not required to seek
alternative work for the first thirty days after his or her dismissal. Sabria v. Department of
Business and Professional Regulation, 15 FCSR 682 (2000). This is commonly referred
to as the initial grace period.
4In Vickery v. Department of Corrections, 30 FCSR 79 (2015), the Commission
held that an employee is entitled to back pay for the entire week in which the Commission
issues the order reinstating the employee to agency employment.
3

BP-2015-010
(Relates to CS-2015-029)
9. For the remaining portion of the back pay exposure period from March 19
through June 26, which covers seventy -three work days, Young is required to provide
evidence that he is entitled to back pay. Typically, this is demonstrated by providing
evidence that an employee conducted a good faith job search.
10. After he was dismissed by the Agency, Young sought unemployment
compensation. Young credibly testified that to be eligible for unemployment benefits he
was required to perform at least five job searches every week. Every week, he was
required to enter information into the computer detailing where he looked for work, when
he looked for work, the type of position that was being applied for, and the status of the
hiring decision.
11. Young credibly testified that he conducted a good faith job search during
the remainder of the back pay exposure period because he was required to apply for at
least five jobs each week to be entitled to unemployment compensation.
12. Young started his job search immediately upon his dismissal, but he was
not immediately approved for unemployment compensation. Most of his applications
were done online or through the People's First System for state jobs. Despite these
applications, Young did not receive any interviews.
13. Young received a total of $3,850.00 in unemployment compensation during
the back pay period. This was the maximum amount that Young was entitled to receive
and the benefit was exhausted.
4

BP-2015-010
(Relates to CS-2015-029)
14. Young provided documentation from Florida Department of Economic
Opportunity showing that he was paid unemployment benefits in ten weeks. The weeks
listed in the documentation were the weeks starting April 13, April 20, April 27, May 4,
May 11, May 18, May 25, June 1, June 8, and June 15, 2015. Young was paid a total of
$2,750.00 for these ten weeks. The difference between the $3,850.00 total amount
Young was paid and the $2,750.00 for the ten weeks expressly listed on the
documentation is $1,100.00. This amount reflects four additional weeks that Young was
eligible to receive unemployment compensation.
15. Young's testimony about his job search, coupled with the supporting
documentation from the Department of Economic Opportunity, provide credible evidence
of a good faith effort to mitigate his job loss. Therefore, Young is entitled to payment for
the remaining portion of the back pay exposure period from March 19 through June 26,
which amounts to $11,090.16 in gross back pay, less taxes and any other lawful
deductions.
16. Young was provided health insurance coverage while he was employed by
the Agency. After he was terminated, his Agency -provided health care coverage lapsed
as of March 31.
17. Young was required by federal law to obtain health insurance coverage for
his family or face tax penalties.
18. Young purchased health insurance from Cigna. His premium was $504.97
per month.
5

BP-2015-010
(Relates to CS-2015-029)
19. Young purchased health insurance for four months, April, May, June, and
July 2015.
20. Young's total cost for health insurance during the back pay period was
$2,019.88.
21. Young was able to return to his state offered insurance through Blue
Cross /Blue Shield starting in August 2015. Young wrote a check for $216.11 in order to
"catch up on the total premiums." Young characterized this as the amount he had to pay
each month before being terminated. According to an email Young entered into
evidence, along with a copy of the check for $216.11, the amount consists of $180.00 for
his August health insurance and $26.11 for the first half of September 2015 dental
insurance.
ANALYSIS
In a back pay proceeding, the Commission is required to approximate the earnings
an employee would have received absent his improper discharge. See Florida State
Lodge, Fraternal Order of Police v. Town of Pembroke Park, 10 FPER If 15001 (1983),
recon. denied, 10 FPER 1115072 (1984), affd in pertinent part, 501 So. 2d 1294 (Fla.
4th DCA 1987).
The parties reached stipulations on many of the variables necessary to calculate
the amount of Young's back pay compensation, such as his rate of pay, work schedule,
and the starting and ending dates for his two grace periods. For the initial grace period,
6

BP-2015-010
(Relates to CS-2015-029)
Young is entitled to $3,342.24 in gross back pay, less taxes and any other lawful
deductions. For the second grace period, Young is entitled to $2,126.88 in gross back
pay, less taxes and any other lawful deductions.
Moreover, he provided documentation from the Department of Economic
Opportunity about the benefits he received that showed he was eligible to receive
unemployment. He was paid the maximum amount allowed, $3,850.00. Therefore, for
the remaining back pay exposure period Young is entitled to $11,090.16 in gross back
pay, less taxes and any other lawful deductions.
In its post- hearing document, the Agency argues that Young should not be entitled
to any back pay outside of the two grace periods because his testimony and
documentation were not precise as to exactly where he applied.5 The Agency recognizes
that the Commission's recent decision in Vickery v. Department of Corrections, 30 FCSR
79 (2015) allowed employees to introduce evidence of unemployment compensation as
evidence of a good faith job search. However, the Agency also suggests that the
Commission's standard on the use of such evidence was "stringent" because the
employee in that case provided testimony as to his job searches, names, dates, and
ways of communication, in addition to evidence of his unemployment. I disagree. The
entire objective behind the Commission's decision in Vickery was to relax an analysis that
had become far too stringent. The Commission specifically held that back pay
5The Agency incorrectly states that he could not remember how many interviews
he went on. Young testified that he did not receive any interviews.
7

BP-2015-010
(Relates to CS-2015-029)
proceedings are remedial in nature and reasonable doubts should be resolved in favor of
the employee because it was the employer's wrongful conduct that initially caused the
loss of employment. Here, in addition to the documentation that Young provided that
showed that he had satisfied the Department of Economic Opportunity's expectations on
seeking employment, Young also credibly testified that he applied to at least five
employers a week, mostly online or through People's First, and that he provided
information on where he applied, when he applied, and the status of his application via
computer to receive his benefit. Under these circumstances, I am satisfied that Young
attempted to mitigate his job loss under the requirements outlined in Vickery.
For the two grace periods and the remaining back pay period, the total amount of
gross back pay is $16,559.28, minus the $3,850 in unemployment compensation he
received. Consequently, Young should be paid a total of $12,709.28 in back pay, less
any taxes and other lawful deductions.
As for Young's out -of- pocket insurance costs, at hearing, the Agency suggested
that Young may not be entitled to any recovery of the amount he spent on health
insurance. However, the Commission has held that employees are entitled to
reimbursement for health insurance coverage as a cornponent of back pay. See Miron v.
Amalgamated Transit Union, Local 1593, 34 FPER IT 268 (2007) (citing Stanfield v.
Department of Health and Rehabilitative Services, 9 FCSR 11196 at 815 (1994)); see also
Smith v. Department of Corrections, 41 FPER 11202 (2014). Young paid a premium of
$504.97 for the four months he was out of work, for a total of $2,019.88. In its post-
8

BP-2015-010
(Relates to CS-2015-029)
hearing filing, the Agency suggests that this amount should be reduced by the amount of
$864.44 ($216.11 /month x 4 months) based on Young's testimony that this represented
the amount that normally would have been withheld from his paycheck for health
insurance had he remained employed. Young's testimony, however, conflicted with the
documentary evidence he provided, which indicated that of the $216.11, only $180 was
attributable to his health insurance premium and the remaining amount appeared to be
for half a month of dental insurance. Therefore, Young is entitled to $2,019.88, minus an
offset of $720 ($180 /month x 4 months), for a total of $1,299.88 to cover the cost of
health insurance above what he would normally have paid had he remained employed by
the Agency.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
1. Young is entitled to $12,709.28 in gross back pay, minus taxes and other
lawful deductions.
2. Young is entitled to $1,299.88 for health insurance costs that occurred
during the back pay period.
RECOMMENDATION
I recommend that the Commission adopt the foregoing recommended order and
award Young back pay and benefits as set forth above.

Any party may file exceptions to my recommended order, but exceptions must be
received by the Commission within fifteen days after the recommended order is issued.
See § 110.227(6), Fla. Stat. (2015); Fla. Admin. Code Rule 28- 106.104 and 28-
106.217(1). The Commission may not change the findings of factor mitigation
recommendation (if any) in this order without first reviewing an official transcript of the
hearing. Any party who desires the Commission to review the transcript must file one
along with the exceptions.
